day-1.t: Day 1 — Set up Canva like a business, not a hobby

b.v: Today's goal

v: Create one business account you will keep
Turn on the settings that stop small annoyances later
Build a folder system so you never lose a design

b.v: About 20 minutes. You can do all of this on a phone, but a laptop is faster for the folder work.

Most people lose hours in Canva not because the tool is hard, but because they started with no plan: designs spread over three accounts, no brand colours saved, and every post built from zero. Today you fix that once.
1) Create the account properly

Use a business email, not your personal one, so a future employee or a family member can be given access without handing over your whole life. Pick a team name that matches your shop, for example Al-Noor Mobile Accessories.

Do this now:|Open canva.com and sign up with your business email|Set the team name to your shop name|Add your logo as the team picture|Write the team description in one line: what you sell and where you are
2) Decide free or paid before you start

The free plan is enough to make good posts. The paid plan (Canva Pro at the time of writing) adds a fuller brand kit, background removal and one-click resizing between sizes. Prices change, so check the current price yourself before you pay monthly for something you may not need.

v: Start free = if you make fewer than about 8 posts a month
Paid makes sense = when resizing one design into four sizes eats your evening every week
Never buy = a yearly plan in your first week, before you know your real workload

b.v: 3) Build a folder system that survives

Canva calls folders Projects. Make one folder per month, and inside it three sub-folders: Raw photos, Working, Final. Files in Final are the ones you actually posted. When your phone fills up or you change staff, this is what saves you.
Create this structure:|Projects → 2026-11|Inside it: 01 Raw photos, 02 Working, 03 Final|Move every old random design into 2026-10 or older
Ctrl+Z=Undo the last change|Ctrl+D=Duplicate the selected element|T=Add a text box|R=Add a rectangle|Ctrl+G=Group selected items so they move together

The most common beginner mistake is designing inside the Home feed and never saving a copy. Always open a design, then use File → Make a copy before you start wrecking a template someone else may also be using.
Practice

Spend 15 minutes: create the account, the month folder and the three sub-folders, then upload one real product photo into 01 Raw photos. Do not design anything yet. Tomorrow you learn the one size that fits Facebook.

day-2.t: Day 2 — Size every design right the first time

b.v: Today's goal

v: Know the four sizes you actually need
Stop text jumping when you resize
Check a design before you post it

b.v: About 20 minutes. Keep this lesson open while you make your four blank sizes.

A sharp design in the wrong size looks amateur. WhatsApp crops the sides of a square post, Facebook hides the bottom of a tall image, and a marketplace listing rejects a photo that is too small. Sizes are the cheapest quality win you have.
1) The four sizes that cover 90 per cent of a small business
Do not collect twenty sizes. Make these four and reuse them. Platform rules change, so treat these as the starting point at the time of writing and check inside the app if a post looks cropped.

v: 1080 × 1080 px = square post, safe for Facebook feed and Instagram feed
1080 × 1350 px = tall feed post, takes more screen space, best for product photos
1080 × 1920 px = story and WhatsApp status, keep text away from top and bottom edges
1200 × 630 px = link preview, the image that appears when someone shares your website

b.v: 2) Resize without breaking the layout
Changing the canvas size by hand always breaks something, because the elements keep their old positions. Resize a copy, then fix three things in this order: the photo, the headline, the logo.

Resize a square post into a story:|Open the square design|File → Make a copy, and rename it with the word Story|Resize the page to 1080 × 1920 (paid plans have a Resize button; on free, duplicate the page and set a custom size)|Pull the photo to fill the new height, then drag the headline down to the middle third|Move the logo up so it sits inside the safe area
Do not stretch a photo to fill a taller frame. Faces become long and bottles become thin, and customers notice instantly. Crop instead of stretch, or place the product on a plain coloured block.
3) Check before you post
Four checks take thirty seconds and save an embarrassed delete. Do them in this order every single time.

v: Read the phone number digit by digit, out loud
Look at the design on your own phone at full brightness, not on the laptop
Check that the price and the old price do not contradict each other
Check the right edge: nothing important within one finger-width of the border

b.v: Practice

Create the four blank sizes as separate designs named with the size in the title. Put one product photo and one headline in each, then send the story version to your own WhatsApp to see how it looks when it fills the screen.

day-3.t: Day 3 — Use templates without looking like a template

b.v: Today's goal

v: Strip a template down to a structure you control
Change five things that make it look custom
Avoid the three looks that scream free template

b.v: About 25 minutes. Pick one template and rebuild it twice.

Your customers see hundreds of Canva posts a day. When they recognise the template, they stop seeing your shop and start seeing a stock design. The fix is not a better template. The fix is using a template only for its layout, then replacing everything else.
1) Take the skeleton, not the skin
A template is two things: a layout (where things sit) and a skin (its colours, fonts and decorations). Keep the layout. Throw away the skin.

Strip it in this order:|Duplicate the template so the original stays clean|Delete every decorative element: blobs, doodles, stickers, background shapes|Delete the sample text and the sample photo|Now look at what is left. That empty arrangement is your layout|Add your photo, your headline, your price, your logo
2) The five changes that make it yours
Do at least four of these five. Two or three is not enough, and the post still reads as stock.

v: Colour = swap the template palette for your two brand colours plus one neutral
Font = replace the display font with the one font you use in every post
Photo = use a real photo of the actual product you are selling, not the stock photo
Shape = change one corner radius or remove one box outline so the geometry differs
Space = add breathing room. Most templates are too tight for a phone screen

b.v: The biggest beginner mistake is keeping the big curved shape and the little sparkle icons because they look nice. Those two elements are exactly what makes a Canva post recognisable from across the room. Delete them.
3) Three looks to avoid
These are the looks that say 'I made this in ten minutes on a free app'. Avoiding them costs you nothing.

v: Five fonts in one image, including one script font for the price
A photo with a busy shop background behind a bottle you are trying to sell
White text on a pale yellow or light grey shape, which nobody can read in sunlight

b.v: Practice

Take one template you like, strip it, and rebuild it with your product. Then make a second version with a different layout but the same colours and fonts. Post the better of the two and keep the other in Working as a spare.

day-4.t: Day 4 — Build a brand kit you will actually follow

b.v: Today's goal

v: Lock three colours and two fonts
Save your logo in the right format
Make every future post start half-finished

b.v: About 20 minutes. This is the highest-value lesson in the course. Do it before you make another post.

A brand is not a logo. It is the fact that a customer can see a post with no name on it and still know it is yours. You get there with repetition: the same two colours, the same two fonts, the same corner for the price. Canva stores this for you so you stop making the decision every time.
1) Choose three colours and write down the codes
One dark colour for text, one strong colour for buttons and prices, one light neutral for backgrounds. That is enough. Do not pick five.

Set the palette:|Pick your main colour, for example a deep green #14532D|Pick one accent that contrasts strongly, for example #F59E0B|Pick a near-white neutral, for example #F8FAFC|Open Brand → Brand Kit and add all three|Write the three codes in your phone notes, so a freelancer or a printer can use them
2) Choose two fonts and never open the font list again

One bold font for headlines, one plain font for everything else. Two is the whole system. If you sell to a broad local market, choose fonts that are easy to read at small sizes on a cheap phone screen.

v: Headline font = heavy, tight, no thin strokes
Body font = simple and wide, readable at 24 px on a phone
For Urdu text = pick a Nastaliq or Naskh font that renders cleanly, and test it at the real size before you commit
Never = a decorative script font for anything a customer must read quickly

b.v: The brand kit on the free plan is limited, and some kit features need a paid plan at the time of writing. That is fine. If the kit is locked, keep a single design called Brand Sheet with your colours, fonts and logo, and copy from it each week. The habit matters more than the feature.
3) Save the logo in the right format
A logo saved as a photo with a white box around it will ruin every coloured background. You want a transparent PNG.

Prepare the logo files:|Upload the original logo to Canva|If it has a white background, remove the background (a paid feature at the time of writing) or ask the person who made the logo for a PNG with transparency|Export as PNG with transparency ticked|Save three versions: full logo with name, mark only, and a white version for dark photos|Put all three in Brand Kit → Logos
Practice

Build the Brand Sheet: three colour swatches with hex codes, two font names in the sizes you will use, and the logo on a light and a dark background. Export it as a PDF and keep it. Any new helper gets this one page and can make on-brand posts from day one.

day-5.t: Day 5 — Text hierarchy: make the eye go where you want

b.v: Today's goal

v: Set three text sizes and stick to them
Learn what belongs on a post and what does not
Fix the contrast problem that kills phone readability

b.v: About 20 minutes. You will rebuild one of your old posts with only three sizes.

Hierarchy means the order in which the eye reads things. On a phone, a customer gives your post about one second. If everything is the same size, the eye finds nothing and scrolls past. Three sizes, used the same way every time, fix this.
1) Three sizes, one job each
Think of it as a shout, a sentence and a whisper. The shout is the headline, the sentence is the detail, the whisper is the small print.

v: Headline = 5 to 8 words, the biggest thing on the design, read from a metre away
Supporting line = one line of fact, roughly a third the size of the headline
Small print = shop name, area, phone number, terms, the smallest readable size
Price = treated as a headline. It is often the second thing a customer looks for

b.v: 2) Write the words before you open Canva
Designers do not type the message into the layout. They write it in a note first, cut it to the bone, then place it. Do this and your posts stop being crowded.

Write in four lines:|Headline: what it is and why now. Example: Winter lawn, new stock|Detail: one useful fact. Example: 3-piece stitched, Rs 4,850|Action: what to do next. Example: WhatsApp to order|Small print: shop name, area, number

Do not paste a full paragraph from your supplier's catalogue. Nobody reads it, and it forces you to shrink the headline to fit. If the text does not fit at the size the headline deserves, the text is too long, not the design.
3) Fix contrast before you export
Contrast is the difference in lightness between your text and its background. Cheap phone screens in daylight wash out low contrast. A quick squint test tells you the truth.

Test any design in 20 seconds:|Hold the phone at arm's length and squint. Can you still read the headline?|If the text sits on a photo, add a dark transparent rectangle behind it|Never put white text on yellow, light green or pale pink|Keep small print out of photos entirely, put it on a solid strip
Practice

Open your worst old post and delete every text box except three: headline, one detail line, one small print line. Set them to 90, 40 and 22 px on a 1080 px wide canvas. Compare the two versions side by side and keep the new one as your template.

day-6.t: Day 6 — Product posts that make people ask the price

b.v: Today's goal

v: Turn a phone photo into a clean product shot
Build one reusable product post layout
Decide what information earns a place on the image

b.v: About 25 minutes. You need three photos of one real product and a plain wall or sheet.
A product post has one job: make the product look worth the money. You do not need a studio. You need even light, a plain background, and a layout you reuse so your feed starts to look organised.
1) Shoot it properly on a phone
The photo matters more than anything you do inside Canva. Ten minutes of setup beats an hour of editing.

Shoot like this:|Put the product near a window, but out of direct sun, in the morning|Tape a plain white chart paper or bedsheet behind it as a backdrop|Turn off the flash and tap the product on screen to focus|Take one wide shot, one close-up of a detail, and one shot with the product in your hand for scale|Do not zoom. Move closer instead
2) One layout, used for every product

Pick a fixed arrangement: product photo filling the top two-thirds, a solid colour band at the bottom, headline at the top left. Repeat it. After six posts, your feed looks like a shop instead of a scrapbook.

v: Top third = product photo, cropped tight, nothing else
Bottom third = colour band with name, key fact, price, WhatsApp number
One corner = your logo, same corner every time
Optional = a small badge such as New or Best seller, one only

b.v: Do not put eleven features on the image. The image sells the look, the caption sells the details. Crowded images get skipped, and the price gets lost among the words.
3) Clean up the photo inside Canva
You can improve a phone photo without Photoshop. Keep it honest: adjusting brightness is fine, changing the colour of the product is not.

Fix the photo:|Select the photo, open Edit image|Raise Brightness slightly and Contrast a little|Use the Background Remover if you want the product on a flat colour (paid feature at the time of writing)|Add a soft shadow shape under the product so it does not float|Export and check it again on the phone
Practice

Shoot one product three ways, build the fixed layout once, then fill it with two products. Save the layout as a template in your account named Product Post Template. From tomorrow, a product post takes four minutes, not forty.

day-7.t: Day 7 — Price offers that are clear and honest

b.v: Today's goal

v: Write a price the customer can read in one glance
Show a discount without breaking trust
Put the terms where they cannot be missed

b.v: About 20 minutes. Have your real prices in front of you, not guesses.

Price is the most-read number on any post, and the most common place small businesses lose trust. A confusing offer makes people suspicious. A clear offer makes them message you. The rules are simple and they never change.
1) Format the price so it reads instantly
Use the same format everywhere: currency, thousands separator, no decimals unless the price has paisa. Say Rs 4,850, not 4850 PKR or Rs.4,850.00.

v: Rs 1,499 = correct and easy to scan
1,499 only = acceptable in a headline, but keep the Rs somewhere visible
Rs.1499/- = looks dated and slows the eye
Rs 1499 PKR only!! = shouting, and the exclamation marks read as a scam

b.v: 2) Show a discount honestly
A discount needs three numbers to be believable: the old price, the new price, and the reason or the deadline. Missing any one of them and the customer assumes the old price was invented.

Build the offer block:|Old price, smaller, with a single line through it|New price, large, in your accent colour|Saving in words: Save Rs 650|One condition line: Till 30 November, or while stock lasts|The condition in a readable size, not 8 px

Never write a discount percentage that does not match the numbers. If old is Rs 2,150 and new is Rs 1,500, that is about 30 per cent, not 40. Customers do this arithmetic while standing in your shop, and getting caught once costs more than the discount.
3) Keep the small print honest and visible
Small print is where trust is either built or destroyed. Keep it short, keep it true, and do not hide it in a corner at 6 px.

v: Delivery charges = state whether included or extra, and roughly how much
Stock = say if a size or colour is limited
Return policy = one short line, exactly as you actually apply it
Location = city and area, because people want to know if they can visit

b.v: Practice

Take one real product and build a proper offer post: old price struck through, new price large, saving written in rupees, one honest condition line, delivery note. Ask a family member to read it for five seconds and tell you the new price. If they cannot, the hierarchy is wrong.

day-8.t: Day 8 — Colours and fonts that suit your market

b.v: Today's goal

v: Pick a palette that works in print and on a phone
Handle Urdu and English text in one design
Stop changing your look every month

b.v: About 20 minutes. Print one test page if you can.

Colour and type carry meaning before a single word is read. In a local market, colour also carries expectations: gold reads as festive, deep red as sale or wedding, green as fresh or grocery. Work with those expectations instead of fighting them.
1) Build a palette with one loud colour
Most beginner palettes fail because all the colours are loud at once. Give one colour the job of shouting and keep the rest quiet.

Build the palette:|Choose one loud colour for prices and buttons|Choose one dark neutral, near-black or deep brown, for text|Choose one warm off-white for backgrounds|Choose one muted second colour for accents only|Check the loud colour against white text. If it is pale, darken it

v: Sale or Eid = one warm loud colour, everything else neutral
Grocery or fresh food = green plus cream, avoid heavy black blocks
Pharmacy or clinic = blue or teal, white background, no gold
Electronics = near-black plus one cool accent, silver-grey neutrals

b.v: 2) Mix Urdu and English without a mess
Many Pakistani shops need both. The trick is to give each language its own line, never mix them inside one sentence, and use a font pair designed for the job.

Set up a bilingual post:|English headline on top, one line|Urdu line below it, right-aligned, its own text box|Use a proper Urdu font, not an English font with Urdu characters forced in|Increase Urdu line spacing slightly, it usually needs more air|Check the Urdu rendering on the phone, because some fonts break on export
Do not type Urdu inside an English text box that has letter spacing or all-caps turned on. The characters join wrongly and the text looks broken to any reader. Give Urdu its own box and its own font.
3) Commit for three months
Recognition comes from repetition. If you change your colours every week because you got bored, customers never learn to spot you. Boredom is the price of consistency, and it is cheap.

v: Review the brand every three months, not every post
Change one thing at a time, then watch whether enquiries move
Keep the old posts. They are your record of what worked

b.v: Practice

Make one bilingual post with an English headline and a separate right-aligned Urdu line. Export it and open it on two different phones, ideally one cheap Android. If the Urdu breaks or the gold disappears in sunlight, change the colour or the font now, not later.

day-9.t: Day 9 — Export correctly so nothing looks cheap

b.v: Today's goal

v: Choose the right file type every time
Keep files small enough for WhatsApp
Export a print-ready file for a banner or flyer

b.v: About 20 minutes. You will export the same design three ways and compare the file sizes.

A beautiful design ruined by a bad export is the most common waste of effort in small business design. Blurry logos, huge files that will not send, and JPGs with grey boxes where transparency should be. Each has one correct fix.
1) Match the file type to the job
There are only four choices that matter. Learn these and you never guess again.

v: PNG = sharp text and flat colour, supports transparency. Use for logos, posts with text, anything with a cut-out product
JPG = smaller files for photos with no transparency. Use for photo-heavy posts when the file must be small
PDF Print = for a printer or press. Use for flyers, banners, shop boards
MP4 = video. Use for reels and status, keep it short and vertical

b.v: 2) Keep the file small enough to send
A 1080 px square PNG with a photo can be 2 to 4 MB. On a weak connection in a shop, that is a failed send. WhatsApp compresses images anyway, so sending a 6 MB file gains you nothing.

Export for WhatsApp and Facebook:|Use Download, then JPG for photo posts and PNG only when you need transparency|Tick the compression option if offered, and compare the result at full size|Aim under 1.5 MB for a feed post|Send to yourself first and open it. If the text is soft, re-export at higher quality
Do not screenshot your design and send the screenshot. Screenshots capture the phone's resolution, the app interface and sometimes your notifications. Always use the Download button.
3) Print files are a different animal

A printer needs a PDF with bleed, which means the design extends slightly past the cut line so no white edge appears after trimming. Ask your printer for their requirement before you design, because every press asks for something slightly different.

Export for print:|Ask the printer: size in inches, bleed, and colour preference|Set a custom size in inches, not pixels|Keep text at least 5 mm inside the edge|Download as PDF Print, and tick the crop marks and bleed option|Ask for one proof copy before the full run
Practice

Export one design three ways: PNG, compressed JPG, and PDF Print. Write down the three file sizes in your notes. Send the compressed JPG to a friend on WhatsApp and ask whether the price is readable on their screen.

day-10.t: Day 10 — A week of content in 45 minutes

b.v: Today's goal

v: Run a repeatable weekly batch
Keep a simple content calendar
Know when Canva is the wrong tool

b.v: About 25 minutes. Do the first batch today, even a rough one.

Posting daily is not a design problem, it is a systems problem. If you design one post at a time, you will stop within three weeks. If you sit down once a week and make five posts in one go, you will still be posting in month six.
1) The 45-minute batch, minute by minute
The trick is to separate thinking from making. Decide all five posts first, then build them without stopping to reconsider.

Run the batch every Sunday evening:|Minutes 1 to 10: choose five posts and write the four-line text for each in your notes|Minutes 11 to 15: open your five saved templates, duplicate each one|Minutes 16 to 35: fill each design. Four minutes each, no font browsing|Minutes 36 to 40: read every phone number and price out loud|Minutes 41 to 45: export all five, put them in the Final folder, schedule or note the posting day

v: Monday = product close-up
Tuesday = price offer
Wednesday = a customer question answered
Thursday = behind the counter or packing photo
Friday = testimonial or reminder

b.v: 2) Keep the calendar brutally simple
You do not need software. A note on your phone with five lines a week is enough, and you will actually use it.

v: One line per day = the post idea in six words
One column = posted or not. Tick it
One line at the bottom = what got the most replies this week
Review monthly = which type of post brought messages, do more of that

b.v: Do not build the batch and post it all in one hour. Five posts dumped together look like spam and reach fewer people. Space them out, one a day, and reply to comments in the first hour.
3) When Canva is not enough
Canva is excellent for posts, flyers, simple catalogues and presentations. It has real limits, and knowing them saves you from a bad result you cannot fix.

v: Precise multi-page documents with references or long tables = use a word processor
Heavy photo retouching, colour correction, product cut-outs with fine hair = use a photo editor
A real website with pages, forms and stock control = use a website builder
Anything a professional press specifies in CMYK with exact colour values = confirm with the printer, they may need a print specialist
Video with careful timing and sound editing = use a video editor

b.v: Practice
Do one full 45-minute batch now: five posts, five templates, exported and named with the date. Then set a repeating reminder for Sunday evening. That reminder is the whole business system.
